Triggers.value: Sleeping alone or in an unfamiliar place

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I imagine getting revenge on the people responsible

Threat.value: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I feel on guard even inside my own home

Memory.value: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things

Negative Appraisals.value: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper
I can't deal with even the slightest upset

vignette: Lata, a 79-year-old South Asian woman and retired airline pilot, has been dealing with the lingering effects of witnessing domestic violence during her childhood. Her symptoms have become increasingly distressing over time, prompting her to seek help now. Lata had always found it difficult to sleep alone or in unfamiliar places, as doing so would often trigger vivid memories of the frightening event she witnessed. These memories felt more real and vivid than those of ordinary things, making it seem like the violence was happening all over again. When Lata experienced these memories, they came in disconnected pieces that did not fit together, which made her feel even more disoriented and distressed. When these triggers occurred, particularly when sleeping alone or encountering certain songs that reminded her of childhood events, she would often turn to maladaptive strategies such as eating excessively or staying up until very late. Lata's excessive eating and delayed sleep were ways for her to manage the intense distress and anxiety triggered by these memories. She had come to believe that these behaviors helped alleviate some of the emotional turmoil. Lata also experienced a heightened sense of irritability, often acting aggressively or having angry outbursts in response to these triggers. This heightened alertness extended beyond just waking up at night; she would feel on guard even inside her own home. These reactions made her question her ability to cope with the slightest upset and reinforced her belief that she was a lousy coper who couldn't rely on herself. The distress and fear associated with her memories led Lata to believe that she could not handle any form of emotional turmoil, which in turn fueled her maladaptive behaviors. Her negative appraisals about her coping abilities were deeply intertwined with the vivid and fragmented memories, making it difficult for her to find solace or peace. Lata's irritability and hypervigilance further contributed to her reliance on eating excessively and staying up late as a way to manage her distress. The constant cycle of triggers leading to maladaptive strategies and negative appraisals created an overwhelming sense of vulnerability and fear in Lata, making it difficult for her to engage fully with life. Her experiences were exacerbated by the fact that she was now retired, and certain aspects of her daily environment would trigger these memories more frequently. For example, working as a pilot meant that hospital smells or environments reminded her of incidents where she had witnessed violence. These triggers reinforced her negative appraisals about herself and contributed to her maladaptive behaviors. The consequences of this cycle were not only emotional but also relational. Lata's irritability and avoidance behaviors began to strain her marriage, leading to frequent misunderstandings and a sense of isolation. Her husband found it increasingly difficult to understand why she was so agitated and often felt helpless in trying to support her. Despite the complexity of these symptoms and their interconnections, what finally brought Lata to seek help was the realization that she could no longer bear the weight of these memories and behaviors on a daily basis. She was most afraid of losing control completely and unable to function as a wife and an individual. At the same time, she hoped for relief from the constant distress and a return to a sense of normalcy in her life. Lata's journey reflects the intricate web of triggers, maladaptive strategies, threat monitoring, memory disturbances, and negative appraisals that have been affecting her over decades. The interplay between these components has created a cycle that she now seeks to break by finding more effective ways to cope with her trauma.
